q_scale.3: good, or mixed with fine highs

_meta.status_rule: Status is recomputed for October 2026 from the window: before window = young; first 15% of window = approachable; 15-50% = peak; 50-80% = mature (plateau); last 20% = drink_up; after window = past. Windows were re-aged from the charts (a 2018 'hold' becomes 'drink' if its window has since opened).
_meta.window_basis: Windows are for the entry's ref_tier (see entries[key].ref_label) from a sound producer and good storage. For another tier, shift additively using the profile in profiles.json: from += tier.ready - ref.ready; to += tier.limit - ref.limit; clamp from >= vintage.
_meta.lookup: Use _by_app[appellation id] to find the chart(s) for an appellation; when two keys are listed, pick by the bottle's colour/style (entries[key].style). Fine units (fine: 1) resolve by walking their parent chain to a covered appellation.

2024.note: Mildew arrived before budbreak and stayed all season, and a drawn-out flowering cut yields. Costly sorting split the vintage: lean, sometimes green lesser wines, but fresh, aromatic, moderate-alcohol grands vins. Margaux, Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe fared better than Pauillac.

2023.note: Heavy spring mildew pressure, then August and September heat. Estates that protected the crop picked a generous harvest of ripe Cabernet with lifted aromatics, fine tannins and freshness. A classically proportioned Left Bank year that will open sooner than 2022.

2022.note: Bordeaux's hottest, driest summer on record should have produced jam, yet old vines on gravel and clay kept their balance. Deep, very tannic, surprisingly fresh wines with long lives ahead. Leave the classed growths alone until the 2030s.

2021.note: April frost, a damp cool summer and mildew made this the most difficult year since 2013. Late-picked Cabernet Sauvignon saved the Médoc: lighter, fresher, lower-alcohol wines in an older Bordeaux idiom that will be ready well before the 2018 to 2020 trio.

2020.note: A wet spring then a long summer drought gave small berries and low yields. The third of a remarkable trilogy: concentrated, tannic, ripe yet fresh Cabernets. Classed growths remain closed and need another five years at least.

2019.note: A hot, dry summer with timely September rain. Ripe, polished, deeply coloured wines with more freshness than the heat suggested and silky tannins. Excellent across the Médoc communes and Pessac-Léognan; still a decade from full maturity at the top.

2018.note: Severe mildew in the wet spring (organic estates lost heavily), then a scorching dry summer. Rich, high-alcohol, opulent wines with big but ripe tannins. The best are monumental; a few feel heavy. Most grands vins are only just emerging from their shell.

2017.note: The April frost hit inland and lower-lying vineyards, while the gravel croupes near the Gironde were largely spared. Medium-bodied, fresh, charming wines that drink earlier than the surrounding vintages. Classed growths are now open for business.

2016.note: A drenched spring, a long drought and saving rain in mid-September produced one of the great Cabernet years: fresh, precise, deeply structured wines. Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe are outstanding. Patience pays: the top wines are still tight.

2015.note: A hot, dry summer gave lush, ripe wines. Margaux had one of its finest years, while September rain in the north of the Médoc made Saint-Estèphe and parts of Pauillac less even. Classed growths are opening up now and will hold for decades.

2014.note: A cool, damp August looked ominous before a glorious September and October ripened the Cabernet. Classic, fresh, well-structured wines of real charm that have been underrated. Classed growths are drinking well and have years at their best ahead.

2013.note: Poor flowering, a wet summer and rot at harvest made the weakest vintage since 1992. Light, lean wines with little substance; even the top estates struggled. Drink any remaining bottles now.

2012.note: A wet spring, hot August and October rain that caught the late Cabernet. The Left Bank is uneven, with better results in Pessac-Léognan and Margaux. Supple, medium-weight wines now in their drinking window.

2011.note: An early, dry spring, a cool summer and a long, uneven ripening. Firm, slightly austere wines with good acidity and sometimes hard tannins. They have softened with age and the best are drinking well, though few will thrill.

2010.note: Dry and sunny with cool nights, producing record tannin levels alongside high alcohol and bright acidity. A monumental, long-lived vintage that was slow to open. The top Médocs are only now becoming approachable and will last half a century.

2009.note: A warm, sunny, even season gave ripe, lush, high-alcohol wines with seductive fruit and plenty of tannin under the plushness. Delicious early and now near their best, though the great estates will keep for decades.

2008.note: Cool and late, then saved by a sunny October that let growers pick small yields of ripe Cabernet. Fresh, classically framed wines with good acidity, long underrated. Fully open now and at a satisfying plateau.

2007.note: A cool, wet summer redeemed only partly by September sun. Light, fruity, early-maturing wines. Even the first growths are near the end of their best; drink up.

2006.note: A hot July, cool August and September rain. Firm, classic, slightly austere Cabernets with good structure; Pessac-Léognan and Pauillac did well. Fully mature now and holding.

2005.note: Dry, sunny and balanced from start to finish. Powerful, concentrated wines with big, ripe tannins and freshness to match. A great vintage that closed down for years; the top estates are just starting their long plateau.

2004.note: A large crop ripened late in a mixed season. Classic, linear, medium-bodied Cabernets with good acidity. Pleasant mature claret today, best drunk over the next few years.

2003.note: The European heatwave. Water-retentive clays in Saint-Estèphe and Pauillac produced some remarkable wines, while elsewhere the fruit tastes cooked and acidity is low. Mature now; drink rather than hold, top estates excepted.

2002.note: Poor flowering and a cool, damp summer, rescued by a fine September that favoured late Cabernet in the Médoc. Lean, classic wines that are now at the end of their window.

2001.note: Cooler than 2000 and overshadowed by it, but fresh, balanced and elegant. The Left Bank is good rather than great. Mature and drinking well now.

2000.note: A warm, dry summer after a difficult spring produced ripe, concentrated, structured wines across both banks. The millennium vintage lived up to its billing: the classed growths are at their peak and the best will last many more years.

1999.note: A generous crop of soft, supple wines. Margaux did particularly well. Early maturing and now at the end of its plateau; drink up.

1998.note: Rain at harvest caught some of the Médoc's Cabernet, leaving firm, sometimes hard wines, while Pessac-Léognan excelled. A Right Bank year above all. Mature now.

1997.note: An early flowering, a wet summer and soft, low-acid wines made for early drinking. Past their best for nearly all estates.

1996.note: A cool year finished by a dry, sunny September that suited late Cabernet. Pauillac and Saint-Julien made magnificent, tannic, long-lived wines. Now fully open and at their best.

1995.note: A hot, dry summer and some September rain. Ripe, firm, well-structured wines on both banks. Fully mature and holding well.

1994.note: A promising hot summer spoiled by September rain. Tannic, hard wines that rarely softened. Most are now past their best.

1993.note: Persistent rain through the harvest gave light, dilute wines with little concentration. A few were pleasant in their first decade; today nearly every bottle is past its best and should be treated as a curiosity.

1992.note: One of the wettest summers in decades swelled the grapes and diluted the wines. Thin, short-lived claret that was best drunk within ten years. Long past; any surviving bottle is a curiosity rather than a pleasure.

1991.note: The frost of 21 April destroyed much of the crop and a wet harvest followed. Small quantities of thin wine. Long past.

1990.note: A hot, dry year with a large crop of ripe, rich, generous wines. Great on both banks. Fully mature, glorious with the right provenance, and holding.

1989.note: A hot, early year of ripe, rich wines; Haut-Brion made a legend. Mature now and drinking beautifully from good cellars.

1988.note: A cool, late season gave classic, firm, tannic wines with good acidity that took decades to soften. Well-kept classed growths are fully mature now and slightly austere; drink them over the next few years rather than wait.

1986.note: A huge crop and a superb Cabernet year in the Médoc. Massively tannic wines that took two decades to open; the best are still vigorous.

1985.note: A severe January freeze was followed by a warm, dry summer and autumn. Ripe, balanced, charming wines that were delicious early and matured gracefully. Most are now on the downslope; drink well-stored bottles soon.

1983.note: A hot, humid summer; Margaux was the star of an otherwise uneven Left Bank. Past its best for most estates.

1982.note: Hot and ripe, with opulent fruit that started a modern collecting culture. The great wines remain splendid, though bottle condition now matters more than the vintage.

1978.note: A cold, late year rescued by a long, sunny autumn, often called a miracle vintage. Classic, firm, medium-bodied wines that drank well for years. Most are now past their best, with first growths the exception.

1975.note: A hot summer produced ripe fruit wrapped in excessively hard tannins. Many wines never came into balance, the fruit fading before the tannin softened. Past its best for nearly all estates, Pomerol aside.

1970.note: A large, healthy crop of classic wines, the first modern vintage of real scale. Most are past their best; well-stored first growths survive.

1966.note: A cool but even season gave firm, elegant, classically proportioned Médoc that aged slowly. Past its best except for the very top estates in impeccable condition, where a lean, cedary charm survives.

1961.note: May frost and poor flowering cut the crop to a fraction, concentrating the rest. One of the century's legends. Surviving bottles in perfect condition can still be extraordinary; drink them.

1959.note: One of the hottest summers of the century produced rich, ripe, generous and long-lived wines, the great forerunner of 1961. Perfectly stored bottles still give enormous pleasure, but the vintage is now a drink-up proposition.

1955.note: A consistent, classic vintage of balanced, well-structured wines, admired for decades but overshadowed by 1953 and 1959. Past its best except for exceptional bottles of first growths with impeccable provenance.

1953.note: Elegant, perfumed, charming wines that were admired from youth and drank beautifully for decades, a favourite of British claret lovers. Mostly past now; a great bottle can still be lovely but fragile once opened.

1949.note: A hot drought year of great quality, rich and long-lived, often ranked alongside 1945 and 1947. Only perfectly stored bottles are still alive, and they should be drunk soon after opening.

1945.note: A May frost cut the crop and a hot summer concentrated the rest. Monumental, long-lived wines; Mouton 1945 is the most famous. Provenance is everything now; drink rather than keep.

2024.note: More a Right Bank year than expected. The limestone plateau and south-facing côtes of Saint-Émilion did best; Pomerol was uneven with tiny yields on the plateau but made some of the vintage's finest wines. Moderate alcohol, fresh, early appeal.

2023.note: Mildew pressure in spring, then late heat. Merlot on Pomerol clay and Saint-Émilion limestone produced generous, aromatic, fresh wines. Very good to excellent at the top, with tannins finer than in 2022.

2022.note: Record heat and drought, yet the cool clay of Pomerol and the limestone of Saint-Émilion kept vines functioning. Deep, ripe, tannic wines with surprising lift. A great Right Bank year to forget in the cellar for now.

2021.note: Frost and mildew hit Merlot hard. Estates rich in Cabernet Franc fared best. Lighter, fresher, lower-alcohol wines in a classical mould, already approachable at the top.

2020.note: Drought from June gave small berries and low yields. Concentrated yet aromatic, silky wines; Pomerol and the Saint-Émilion plateau are superb. Hold.

2019.note: Hot and dry with welcome September rain. Ripe, silky, balanced wines with lovely freshness on limestone. Top estates need a few more years.

2018.note: Spring mildew then a hot, dry summer. Rich, opulent, sometimes very alcoholic Merlot. The best are magnificent; a few are heavy. Hold.

2017.note: The April frost devastated lower-lying vineyards and satellites, while the Pomerol plateau and Saint-Émilion côtes escaped. Fresh, medium-weight, charming wines from the spared estates, now open.

2016.note: A long drought broken by mid-September rain. Fresh, precise, fragrant Right Bank wines with fine tannins. Opening now, with decades ahead.

2015.note: A hot, dry summer that suited Merlot perfectly. Pomerol and Saint-Émilion made lush, ripe, great wines. Opening now and will hold for decades.

2014.note: A cool, grey August gave way to a fine September and October that rescued the Merlot. Fresh, supple, attractive wines of moderate weight, good value from the start and drinking well now.

2013.note: Poor flowering, a wet summer and rot at harvest made a tiny, difficult vintage on the Right Bank as elsewhere. Light, sometimes dilute wines with short lives; drink any remaining bottles now.

2012.note: Merlot ripened before October rain caught the Cabernet, so Pomerol and Saint-Émilion outshone the Médoc. Supple, rich wines at their peak.

2011.note: A hot, dry spring, a cool summer and uneven ripening gave firm, sometimes rustic wines with drying tannins. The best Pomerols and limestone Saint-Émilions are pleasing and fully mature now; no reason to wait.

2010.note: A dry, sunny year with cool nights gave high alcohol, high tannin and high acidity, all in balance. Massive, long-lived Merlot and Cabernet Franc that are only now becoming approachable at the top estates.

2009.note: A warm, sunny, even season gave lush, generous, plush Merlot with plenty of ripe tannin underneath. Seductive young and drinking beautifully now, with the top Pomerols holding for decades.

2008.note: A late, cool year saved by a sunny October that let growers pick small yields of ripe Merlot. Fresh, mid-weight wines with good acidity, long overlooked and now fully mature.

2007.note: A cool, wet summer redeemed only partly by September sun gave light, soft, early-drinking wines. Even the top estates are past their best; finish any bottles left.

2006.note: A hot July, cool August and September rain, but Merlot on the Pomerol plateau was largely picked before the damage. Pomerol was outstanding, Saint-Émilion more variable. Fully mature and drinking well now.

2005.note: A dry, sunny, balanced year from start to finish. Concentrated, structured, long-lived Right Bank wines with deep fruit and firm tannin, now at the beginning of a long peak.

2004.note: A large crop ripened late in a mixed season, giving classic, fresh, medium-bodied wines. Pleasant and fully mature now; drink over the next few years.

2003.note: Heatwave Merlot often tastes baked and low in acidity, though cool limestone sites in Saint-Émilion and some Pomerol clays held freshness. Few will improve; drink up.

2002.note: Coulure and millerandage at flowering cut the Merlot crop, and a cool summer followed. Light, lean wines that were best young. Past now for all but a few top estates.

2001.note: Cooler than 2000 and overshadowed by it, but elegant, balanced and fresh, a better Right Bank year than many realised. Pomerol and Saint-Émilion are mature, harmonious and holding well.

2000.note: A difficult spring then a warm, dry summer gave ripe, concentrated, structured wines of great quality on both banks. The top Right Bank estates are at their peak now and will hold for many years.

1999.note: A September hailstorm struck part of Saint-Émilion; elsewhere a generous crop gave soft, supple Merlot. Attractive in youth and now at the end of its plateau; drink up.

1998.note: Merlot ripened fully before the rains that troubled the Médoc Cabernet. Pomerol and Saint-Émilion made great, rich, plush wines, the finest Right Bank year of the decade, now mature and still splendid.

1997.note: An early flowering and a wet summer gave soft, low-acid wines intended for early drinking and sold at inflated prices. Past their best for nearly all estates.

1996.note: A cool year finished by a dry September that favoured late-ripening Cabernet. Right Bank Merlot was less consistent, though Cabernet Franc estates did well. Drink up now.

1995.note: A hot, dry summer and some September rain gave ripe, firm, well-structured wines across Pomerol and Saint-Émilion. Fully mature and holding, with no need to keep them longer.

1994.note: A hot summer, then September rain; Merlot was largely picked before the worst of it. Some solid, firm Pomerols resulted, but most wines are past their best now.

1993.note: A wet harvest gave light, lean wines, though a few Pomerols surprised with their charm and longevity. Past for nearly all; any remaining bottles are curiosities.

1992.note: One of the wettest summers in decades swelled the berries and diluted the wines. Short-lived Right Bank wines that were best within a decade. Long past.

1991.note: The frost of 21 April wiped out much of the Right Bank crop and several leading estates made no grand vin at all. What little was bottled was light and is now long past.

1990.note: A hot, dry year with a large crop of rich, ripe, great wines on both banks. Fully mature, glorious from good cellars and holding well.

1989.note: A hot, early year of opulent, ripe Merlot with soft tannins; Pétrus and the top Pomerols are legendary. Mature and drinking beautifully from good cellars.

1985.note: A severe winter freeze damaged some vines, then a warm, dry season gave ripe, charming, balanced wines. Matured gracefully; drink up soon from good provenance.

1982.note: A hot, ripe year of opulent, plush wines that became legends in Pomerol and helped launch modern Bordeaux collecting. Fully mature; drink up from good provenance.

1975.note: A hot year of hard tannins in the Médoc but real success in Pomerol, where the clay gave depth and Pétrus made a great wine. Past for most estates now.

1964.note: Pomerol and Saint-Émilion picked their Merlot before the October deluge that ruined much of the late Médoc harvest. Fine Right Bank wines resulted, but most bottles are past their best now.

1961.note: May frost and poor flowering left a tiny crop of legendary concentration; Pétrus and Latour à Pomerol 1961 are mythical. Perfectly stored bottles are still remarkable; drink them rather than keep them.

1947.note: A torrid summer produced Cheval Blanc 1947, famously rich, high in alcohol and almost port-like, plus great Pomerols. Many bottles are reconditioned or fake, so provenance decides everything now.

2024.note: A season of mildew and uneven flowering. The best Sauternes and Barsac are excellent, but the vintage is more uneven than hoped and many wines lack the acidity that keeps their sweetness lively. Choose producers with care.

2023.note: A warm summer and a humid, sunny autumn brought clean botrytis in good time. Fresh, pure, well-balanced wines that will be delicious young yet have the acidity to age for decades.

2022.note: Drought and heat held botrytis back until autumn humidity brought it on. Rich, concentrated, golden wines with more freshness than the summer suggested at the leading châteaux.

2021.note: April frost slashed the crop, some estates losing most of it, and the cool summer delayed ripening. Small volumes of fresh, lively, lighter wines with good acidity, already pleasant.

2020.note: Spring mildew and a summer drought reduced the crop, and botrytis was patchy. Fresh, elegant, mid-weight wines that are pleasurable now and will keep for decades at the top.

2019.note: A hot summer, then autumn rain and sun that brought clean, even botrytis. Balanced, fresh, pure Sauternes with lovely tension, already delicious and with a long life ahead.

2018.note: Spring mildew and summer hail reduced the crop before a hot, dry finish. Rich, ripe wines, uneven across the appellation; the best are generous and opulent.

2017.note: Early, abundant, clean botrytis, helped by September rain on a ripe crop, made a great vintage of pure, intense and beautifully balanced wines. Long-lived and already thrilling.

2016.note: A dry summer delayed botrytis, which arrived late and cleanly. Fresh, elegant, lacy wines with fine acidity, drinking well already and built for the long haul.

2015.note: A hot summer, then perfect alternation of rain and sun for botrytis. Rich, concentrated, great wines with freshness and complexity, among the finest of the decade.

2014.note: A cool summer and a fine, long autumn gave pure, lively, fresh wines with clean botrytis. Delicious now and well placed for decades.

2013.note: A miserable year for red Bordeaux turned out well for botrytis, which spread quickly in the damp autumn. Pure, fresh, well-balanced Sauternes, underrated and drinking nicely.

2012.note: Rain and grey rot ruined much of the crop and Château d'Yquem made no wine at all. Few wines of note; those released are light and should be drunk.

2011.note: A hot spring and early, abundant botrytis made rich, intense, great wines with good acidity. Approachable now but built for many decades in the cellar.

2010.note: A dry, cool-nighted year gave clean botrytis and high acidity. Pure, racy wines with tension and precision, drinking well, with a long life ahead.

2009.note: A warm year with rapid, rich botrytis produced opulent, great, deeply concentrated wines. At an early peak, gaining complexity for decades.

2008.note: A cool year with a small crop and late botrytis. Fresh, mid-weight wines with good acidity; good rather than great, and mature now.

2007.note: A poor year for reds but a very good one for Sauternes, with a fine autumn and clean botrytis. Fresh, fine, aromatic wines at their peak.

2006.note: A hot July, a cool August and a rapid, sometimes rot-affected botrytis. Rich but uneven wines; the best are generous and mature now.

2005.note: A dry year with late but concentrated botrytis gave rich, powerful wines; Yquem was superb. At their peak and holding.

2004.note: A large, late crop gave good, mid-weight wines with moderate botrytis. Pleasant, mature and best drunk over the next few years.

2003.note: The heatwave produced early, very rich, heavy wines with low acidity; the best have surprising freshness.  Mature and opulent; drink over the next decade while the fruit is still vivid.

2002.note: A cool year rescued by a fine September and October gave good, balanced wines with clean fruit. Mature; drink over the next few years.

2001.note: A legendary year: pure, intense botrytis and electric acidity in perfect balance. Yquem 2001 is among the greatest modern Sauternes. At its peak with decades to go.

2000.note: Superb for red Bordeaux, but October rain spoiled the botrytis harvest just as it began. Weak, dilute wines from most estates, now past their best.

1999.note: A warm summer and a variable autumn gave good, balanced wines with decent botrytis. Mature now and best drunk over the next few years.

1998.note: A hot August and a mixed autumn gave good, rich wines, sometimes lacking finesse. Mature and holding at the top estates.

1997.note: A long, warm autumn with abundant botrytis gave rich, very good wines, overlooked because of the weak reds. Mature and generous.

1996.note: A cool summer and a fine autumn gave fresh, elegant, very good wines with lively acidity. Mature and holding well.

1995.note: A hot summer and a reasonable autumn gave good, balanced wines with moderate botrytis character. Mature now; drink over the next few years.

1994.note: A promising summer was undone by September and October rain. Light, uneven wines; past their best for nearly all estates.

1993.note: A very wet autumn ruined the botrytis, many estates declassified their crop, and some top châteaux released no grand vin. Poor, thin wines, long past.

1992.note: A wet, cool summer and a rainy harvest gave dilute wines with little botrytis; Yquem chose not to release a 1992. Light wines, long past their best.

1991.note: The April frost cut the crop and the autumn was mixed. Small quantities of light, early-maturing wines with modest botrytis. Past their best now.

1990.note: The third of a great trio: a hot year with abundant botrytis giving rich, powerful, great wines. Mature and splendid, with plenty of life left.

1989.note: A hot, early year of opulent, great wines with deep botrytis character and plenty of alcohol. Mature, splendid and holding for many years yet.

1988.note: Classic, pure, perfectly botrytised wines with great freshness, the finest of the late 1980s trio for many tasters. Mature and holding beautifully.

1986.note: Ideal alternation of autumn mist and sun spread clean botrytis widely, producing great, intense, complex wines. Mature and splendid from good cellars.

1983.note: A warm, humid autumn gave abundant botrytis and rich, very good wines. Mature and still lively at the top estates.

1976.note: A hot drought summer and an early harvest gave rich, ripe, golden wines. Mature now; the best are still lovely.

1975.note: A good year for botrytis gave fine, balanced wines with lively acidity and good concentration. Mature and holding at the leading châteaux.

1971.note: Elegant, well-balanced wines with good acidity and clean botrytis, often preferred to the reds of the year. Mature and still fine.

1967.note: A great Sauternes year in a modest one for reds, with Yquem 1967 a legend. Mature and still splendid from good cellars.

1959.note: A hot, sunny year produced great, rich, deeply botrytised wines of real power. Mature, amber and still vigorous when well stored.

1955.note: A fine, balanced vintage for sweet Bordeaux, overshadowed by 1959 but long-lived. Mature; well-kept bottles show great complexity of orange peel, caramel and spice.

1945.note: A May frost left a tiny crop that a hot summer concentrated into great, powerful wines. Mature; provenance decides everything at this age.

1937.note: A legendary Sauternes year with remarkable acidity and concentration, still cited as a benchmark. Mature; provenance decides everything at this age.

1929.note: A hot, legendary year for Sauternes, rich and long-lived, made just before the Depression. Mature; provenance decides everything at this age.

1921.note: A hot year that many rank as the greatest Sauternes vintage of the century. Mature; provenance decides everything at this age.

2024.note: April frost, endless spring rain, mildew and hail made one of the hardest seasons in memory and a very small crop. Careful growers made light, fragrant, crunchy reds with modest alcohol that will drink early.

2023.note: A huge crop ripened in a hot August and early September. Where yields were held back, the reds are fleshy, ripe and charming with fine tannins; over-cropped wines are dilute. Expect early appeal.

2022.note: Heat and drought but well-timed rain gave a healthy, generous crop. Ripe, fresh, well-balanced reds with silky tannins and real depth, a rare combination of quality and quantity. Keep the premiers crus until 2028 or so.

2021.note: The April frost and a cool, wet summer slashed yields and brought mildew. Light, transparent, fragrant reds in an old-fashioned key with bright acidity. Many premiers crus are open already; grand crus need longer.

2020.note: One of the earliest harvests on record, often in August, after a dry, hot summer. Small berries, concentrated, structured wines that kept surprising freshness. Built for the cellar; still closed.

2019.note: Frost, coulure and two heatwaves cut the crop, but the reds are ripe, concentrated and vibrant, with fine tannins. A great vintage that is still in its youthful phase.

2018.note: A hot, dry summer with a large crop. Ripe, generous, sometimes high-alcohol reds; those who picked early made fresh, delicious wines. Approachable now and will hold.

2017.note: A healthy, generous crop after a frost scare. Charming, open, consistent reds of medium weight with lovely fruit, for drinking rather than long keeping. At their best now.

2016.note: The frost of 27 April devastated parts of the Côte, especially Chambolle, Marsannay and the Côte de Beaune. What survived made pure, fresh, classic reds with fine structure. Opening now.

2015.note: A hot, dry year that produced ripe, concentrated, deeply coloured reds with plenty of tannin and better acidity than feared. A great vintage now entering its window.

2014.note: Hail struck Beaune, Pommard and Volnay again in June, and fruit flies troubled the harvest. Fresh, pretty, lighter reds with good balance, at their peak now.

2013.note: A cold spring, hail in the Côte de Beaune and an October harvest. Lean, fresh, classic reds with high acidity; the Côte de Nuits did better. Mature now.

2012.note: Poor flowering, hail and mildew left a tiny crop of concentrated, intense, very good reds. Drinking well now with years to go at the top.

2011.note: An early spring, a cool summer and an early harvest gave uneven, light reds, sometimes with green, stemmy notes. Charming at best; drink up now.

2010.note: A cold winter and poor flowering cut yields; the result was intense, vibrant, high-acid reds of great purity and depth. A great classic vintage now at its peak.

2009.note: A warm, sunny, healthy year gave ripe, round, generous reds with soft tannins; some lack acidity and feel heavy. Fully mature and delicious now; no reason to wait.

2008.character: cool, saved by the north wind
2008.note: A cool, damp summer brought rot, until drying north winds in September saved the crop. High-acid, fresh, classic reds that needed time and are now mature.

2007.note: An early spring and a wet, grey summer gave light, early-drinking reds with pretty fruit and little depth. Premiers crus are past their best; finish them.

2006.note: A hot July, a cool damp August and rot at harvest gave uneven reds; the Côte de Nuits did better than the Côte de Beaune. Drink up now.

2005.note: A dry, sunny, healthy season gave deep, structured, great reds with ripe tannins and fine acidity. They were closed for years and are now in their long window. Grand crus from great cellars hold several years longer.

2004.note: Hail and a ladybird infestation at harvest left some wines with green, vegetal notes. Light, lean reds that were best young and are now past their best.

2003.note: The heatwave and an August harvest produced atypical, low-acid, very ripe reds; some Côte de Nuits wines are remarkable, others taste cooked. Mature; drink up.

2002.note: A cool summer and a sunny, dry September with north winds gave fine, balanced, classic reds with good concentration. Mature and drinking well now. Grand crus from great cellars hold several years longer.

2001.note: A cool year with a wet September gave light, fresh, perfumed reds; the Côte de Nuits did best. Premiers crus are at the end of their plateau; drink up.

2000.note: Rain at harvest diluted the crop and the Côte de Beaune suffered most. Light, early-maturing reds that are now past their best.

1999.note: A large crop ripened in a warm, dry summer and gave ripe, concentrated, great reds with fine tannins. Mature and still vigorous, especially in the Côte de Nuits. Grand crus from great cellars hold several years longer.

1998.note: Frost, hail and sunburn, then September rain, gave firm, sometimes hard reds whose tannins softened slowly. Mature; drink up over the next couple of years.

1997.note: A warm, sunny year of soft, ripe, low-acid reds that were lovely early. Premiers crus are now past their best; grand crus are fading.

1996.note: Ripe fruit and very high acidity from a cool, sunny, windy season. Structured, long-lived reds, though some never fully opened. Mature now. Grand crus from great cellars hold several years longer.

1995.note: A small crop of firm, structured, deeply coloured reds after poor flowering. Mature now; drink up the premiers crus while they keep their fruit.

1994.note: A promising summer undone by harvest rain that diluted the wines and brought rot. Light reds, long past their best.

1993.note: A wet summer, but thick-skinned, healthy fruit in the Côte de Nuits made dark, structured, long-lived reds that were dismissed early and aged superbly. Drink up the premiers crus now.

1992.note: A large crop and a rainy harvest gave light, soft, forward reds for early drinking. A few Côte de Nuits wines had charm, but the vintage is long past its best.

1991.note: Hail in the Côte de Nuits reduced a small crop of firm, concentrated reds that outshone their reputation. Past their best for premiers crus.

1990.note: A warm, dry year of ripe, concentrated, great reds with sweet fruit and firm structure. Premiers crus should be drunk now; grand crus from good cellars are holding.

1989.note: A warm year of ripe, soft, charming reds with lower acidity than 1988 or 1990. Premiers crus are past their best; well-kept grand crus survive.

1988.note: Firm, tannic, high-acid reds that took decades to open and rewarded patience. Premiers crus are at the end of the road; drink up. Grand crus from great cellars hold several years longer.

1985.note: A frosty winter, then a warm, ripe summer gave charming, fleshy reds admired from youth. Past for most premiers crus; grand crus from great cellars still delight.

1978.note: A cold, late season rescued by a superb September gave a small crop of great, balanced reds. Past for premiers crus; grand crus from top domaines remain sublime.

1971.note: Hail and poor flowering left a small crop of rich, concentrated reds. Long past for premiers crus; only the greatest grand crus in perfect condition survive.

1969.note: A small, great vintage of concentration and balance, long a collector favourite. Past for premiers crus; perfectly stored grand crus can still be wonderful.

1959.note: A hot summer gave rich, ripe, great reds. Past for premiers crus; only grand crus with perfect provenance are still worth opening.

1945.note: Frost and hail left a tiny, legendary crop, the last Romanée-Conti before replanting. Treat surviving bottles as historic artefacts whose condition matters more than the vintage.

2024.note: Frost, rain, mildew and hail cut the crop to a fraction in places, but whites came through better than reds. Fresh, precise, mid-weight Chardonnay with lively acidity; buy from growers who sorted hard.

2023.note: A record-sized crop ripened in late-summer heat. Ripe, open, generous whites with soft acidity; the best growers limited yields and made wines of depth, while others are dilute. Early drinking.

2022.note: A hot, dry summer with timely rain gave a healthy, generous crop. Ripe yet balanced whites with good energy and texture, very good across the Côte de Beaune and Mâconnais.

2021.note: The April frost destroyed much of the Chardonnay crop in Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne. What remained made tense, classic, bright whites with lovely cut, in tiny quantities.

2020.note: A drought year and a very early harvest gave concentrated whites that kept surprising freshness thanks to early picking. Rich but well balanced; the premiers crus are opening now.

2019.note: Frost and heat reduced yields. Rich, ripe whites with more vibrancy than the heat suggested, generous and full. At their best over the next few years.

2018.note: A hot year and a big crop. Ripe, plump whites, sometimes low in acidity; early pickers made the freshest wines. Drink over the next few years.

2017.note: A healthy, generous crop of beautifully balanced, classic whites with ripe fruit and fine acidity. An excellent white vintage, drinking well and holding.

2016.note: The April frost cut yields severely, but the surviving grapes made pure, balanced, focused whites with good acidity. Mature and drinking well now.

2015.note: A hot, dry summer gave rich, broad, lower-acid whites, more successful on cooler, higher sites. Drink now while the fruit is generous.

2014.note: Hail hit parts of the Côte de Beaune, but the whites are tense, mineral and concentrated, a great classic vintage. At its peak now and holding.

2013.note: A cold spring, hail and a late October harvest gave lean, tense, sometimes botrytis-touched whites in small volumes. Drink up now.

2012.note: Poor flowering, hail and oidium left a small crop of rich, concentrated whites with fresh acidity. Mature and holding well.

2011.note: An early, uneven year with a cool summer gave soft, easy, attractive whites for early drinking. Past their best now for most premiers crus.

2010.note: A cold winter and poor flowering gave a small crop of tense, concentrated, great whites with superb acidity. Mature and splendid now. Grand crus from great cellars hold several years longer.

2009.note: A warm, sunny year of rich, round, low-acid whites that charmed early. Past their best now for most premiers crus; drink any remaining bottles.

2008.note: A cool year saved by north winds gave intense, high-acid whites, some with botrytis notes. Long-lived for the era; drink up the premiers crus soon.

2007.note: Better for whites than reds: fresh, elegant, mineral Chardonnay from a cool summer. Past its best for most premiers crus; grand crus can still be lovely.

2006.note: A warm July and a mixed August gave rich, broad, early-maturing whites. Past their best now; any remaining bottles should be drunk. Premature oxidation struck many white Burgundies of this era, so open bottles with caution.

2005.note: A dry, sunny year gave rich, structured, concentrated whites in a great red vintage. Drink up. Premature oxidation struck many white Burgundies of this era, so open bottles with caution.

2004.note: A cool, late year better for whites than reds gave fresh, classic, mineral Chardonnay. Past its best for premiers crus now. Premature oxidation struck many white Burgundies of this era, so open bottles with caution.

2003.note: The heatwave and an August harvest made heavy, low-acid, sometimes flabby whites that lacked the tension Chardonnay needs to age. Long past their best.

2002.note: A great white vintage of balance, ripeness and concentration after a sunny, windy September. Drink up. Premature oxidation struck many white Burgundies of this era, so open bottles with caution.

2001.note: A cool year with a wet September gave lean, early-maturing whites of modest depth and some dilution. Past their best now, grand crus included.

2000.note: A warm summer gave ripe, attractive, generous whites. Past their best now for premiers crus. Premature oxidation struck many white Burgundies of this era, so open bottles with caution.

1999.note: A large crop of ripe, attractive whites, sometimes lacking concentration. Past for most premiers crus. Premature oxidation struck many white Burgundies of this era, so open bottles with caution.

1998.note: Spring frost, hail and uneven ripening gave patchy whites of modest quality and short lives. Long past their best; treat surviving bottles as curiosities.

1997.note: A warm, sunny year of ripe, soft, low-acid whites that were delicious young and made for early drinking. Past their best now.

1996.note: Great, high-acid whites from a cool, sunny, windy season, famously the vintage in which premature oxidation was first widely noticed. Past for most; sound bottles survive.

1995.note: A small crop of concentrated, rich whites with good acidity. Past for most premiers crus. Premature oxidation struck many white Burgundies of this era, so open bottles with caution.

1994.note: A promising summer ended in harvest rain that diluted the crop and spread rot. Light, short-lived whites, long past their best.

1993.note: A wet summer and rot at harvest gave dilute, uneven whites that never had the stuffing to age. Long past their best.

1992.note: A big crop of ripe, rich, early-charming whites, better than the reds of the year. Past for premiers crus now.

1991.note: A small, uneven crop after spring frost and summer hail, overshadowed by stronger years either side. Past its best for every tier now.

1990.note: A warm year of ripe, generous whites overshadowed by the reds. Past for premiers crus; grand crus from great cellars survive.

1989.note: A hot year of rich, great, opulent whites. Past for premiers crus; grand crus from top domaines can still impress.

1986.note: A wet September brought rot and botrytis, giving rich, sometimes botrytis-tinged whites of real opulence. Past for nearly all premiers crus; grand crus are fading.

1985.note: A warm, sunny year of great, balanced, concentrated whites. Past for premiers crus; grand crus from great cellars still delight.

1978.note: A late, small crop of great, long-lived whites with high acidity. Past for premiers crus; perfectly stored grand crus remain extraordinary.

2024.note: Frost, hail and relentless mildew cut Chablis yields drastically, some estates losing most of the crop. Light, fresh, saline wines in very small quantities; drink the premiers crus young.

2023.note: A large crop ripened fully in a warm September. Ripe, open, approachable wines with softer acidity than usual; some are dilute, the best are generous and saline.

2022.note: A hot, dry year with a healthy, generous crop. Ripe yet balanced Chablis with good salinity and energy, very good across premiers and grands crus.

2021.note: Frost devastated the crop, but the survivors are steely, tense, classic Chablis with superb cut and oyster-shell salinity. Tiny quantities; premiers crus are opening.

2020.note: A hot, early year, yet the wines show ripe fruit framed by good tension and chalky grip. Very good, drinking well now and holding.

2019.note: Frost and a hot summer reduced yields and concentrated the wines. Ripe, energetic, mouth-filling Chablis with good acidity behind the fruit, now at its peak.

2018.note: A big crop ripened in a hot summer, giving round, generous wines, less steely and typical than usual. Drink now.

2017.note: Frost in April and hail in May reduced yields, but the wines are classic, fresh and mineral with good depth. At their peak now.

2016.note: Frost in April and repeated hail storms made a tiny crop of balanced, concentrated wines with good acidity. Mature now and drinking well.

2015.note: A hot, dry year of rich, broad Chablis with ripe fruit and less steel than usual. Drink now while it is generous.

2014.note: Hail touched some slopes, but this is a great classic vintage of tension, salinity and depth. At its peak and holding for years.

2013.note: Hail in summer and rot at a late harvest made a difficult year with lean, uneven wines. Past their best.

2012.note: Hail and poor flowering left a small crop of concentrated, classic Chablis with fine acidity and saline length. Mature and holding at the top.

2011.note: An early, warm spring and a cool summer gave soft, easy, early-maturing Chablis with modest acidity. Past its best now for premiers crus.

2010.note: A small crop of tense, concentrated, great Chablis with superb acidity and depth. Mature and splendid; grand crus have many years left.

2009.note: A warm, sunny year of ripe, soft, generous Chablis with lower acidity than usual. Charming young, now past its best for premiers crus.

2008.note: A cool year of high acidity, intensity and purity, a great classic that needed time. Mature now and still vibrant.

2007.note: A cool, damp summer and a fine September gave fresh, mineral, classic Chablis with bright acidity. Drink up the premiers crus; grand crus are holding.

2006.note: A warm July, a cool August and some rot gave ripe, early-maturing wines with soft acidity. Past their best now.

2005.note: A dry, sunny year gave rich, concentrated Chablis with good structure and depth. Premiers crus are at the end of their plateau; drink up.

2004.note: A large crop of fresh, light, classic wines from a cool, late season. Pleasant in youth and past their best now.

2003.note: Spring frost cut the crop, then the heatwave produced broad, soft, low-acid wines untypical of Chablis. Long past their best.

2002.note: A great, balanced vintage of ripeness and tension. Premiers crus are at the end of their window; grand crus still shine.

2001.note: Hail in summer and rot at a wet harvest gave dilute, uneven wines with little concentration or grip. Long past their best at every level.

2000.note: A warm summer gave ripe, attractive Chablis with good balance and early charm. Past its best now for premiers crus.

1999.note: A large crop of attractive, early-maturing wines with soft fruit and moderate acidity, pleasant in their first decade. Past its best now.

1998.note: Spring frost and summer hail made an uneven year, with some fine wines from the best slopes. Past its best now.

1997.note: A warm year of soft, ripe, low-acid Chablis that drank well young but lacked the steel for long ageing. Past its best now.

1996.note: A cool, sunny, windy year gave great, high-acid, long-lived Chablis. Drink up the premiers crus; grand crus can still impress.

1995.note: A small crop of concentrated, firm wines with good acidity, slow to open. Past its best now for premiers crus.

1994.note: Harvest rain diluted the crop and brought rot to the Serein valley. Light, short-lived Chablis, long past its best at every level.

1993.note: A wet season and rot at harvest made uneven, lean wines with some success on the grand cru slope. Past their best now for all tiers.

1992.note: A ripe, generous, attractive vintage for early drinking, better than its reputation at the time. Past its best now, grand crus included.

1991.note: Spring frost reduced the crop and the surviving wines were light and lean, overshadowed by 1990. Long past their best.

1990.note: A warm year of great, rich, balanced Chablis with real depth. Past for premiers crus; grand crus from top cellars such as Raveneau and Dauvissat survive.

2024.note: A wet, cool year of frost, hail and the worst downy mildew in decades slashed yields. Quality of the surviving fruit was decent, but expect few houses to declare a vintage.

2023.note: A record-breaking crop with huge bunches, then a heatwave during harvest and some rot. Variable quality; selective houses may declare, especially for Chardonnay.

2022.note: A hot, dry, healthy season gave a large crop of ripe, balanced grapes with good acidity. Widely expected to be a major declared vintage.

2021.note: April frost, a wet summer and mildew made one of the most difficult years in decades. High acidity and tiny volumes; few vintage wines.

2020.note: A hot, dry, early year with healthy fruit gave ripe wines with better acidity than expected. Many houses are expected to declare.

2019.note: Heatwaves and a small crop gave concentrated, balanced wines with good acidity and real depth. A strong vintage now being released; give it a few more years.

2018.note: A hot summer and a huge, healthy crop gave ripe, generous wines; Pinot Noir excelled. Vintage wines are on the market now.

2017.note: Rain and rot at harvest, especially in Pinot Meunier, made a difficult year. Few houses declared; drink the vintage wines that were released.

2016.note: Frost, hail and mildew cut yields, then a hot August ripened good Pinot Noir. Some fine vintage wines, often Pinot-led, now on release.

2015.note: A hot, dry summer gave rich, ripe wines; some show a slightly bitter, drought-marked edge. Widely declared and drinking from release.

2014.note: A wet August and fruit-fly problems were rescued by a sunny September. Chardonnay fared best and made some good vintage wines.

2013.note: A cold spring and a rare October harvest gave classic, high-acid, slow-maturing wines; Chardonnay is outstanding. Long-lived and still opening.

2012.note: Frost, hail and mildew cut the crop drastically, but the remaining fruit was ripe and concentrated. A great vintage with great Pinot Noir.

2011.note: An early, warm spring and a cool, damp summer brought rot and green notes. Few vintage wines were made; drink any you have.

2010.note: Heavy August rain caused rot, especially in Pinot Meunier and Pinot Noir; Chardonnay was better. Few vintages were declared; drink them.

2009.note: A sunny, warm year of ripe, generous, approachable vintage wines with soft acidity. At their peak now and lovely to drink.

2008.note: A cool, overcast summer and a sunny September gave classic, high-acid, great wines that have aged slowly. Just reaching their peak.

2007.note: An early spring and a cool August gave elegant, lighter wines; Chardonnay was best. Mature now and best drunk soon.

2006.note: A hot July and a cool August, then a fine September, gave ripe, generous, rounded wines. Mature and drinking well now.

2005.note: Rain at harvest brought rot, and Pinot Noir fared better than Chardonnay. Uneven vintage wines, now mature and best drunk.

2004.note: A large, healthy crop of elegant, classic, long-lived wines in which Chardonnay excelled. At its peak now, with prestige cuvées holding for years.

2003.note: April frost and the heatwave made a tiny, very early crop of rich, low-acid wines. Few vintages were declared; drink them.

2002.note: A warm, sunny, dry season gave great, ripe, balanced wines, widely declared by the leading houses. At its peak now and holding.

2001.note: The wettest year in decades gave a poor, rot-affected harvest. Hardly any vintage wine was made, and what exists is past its best.

2000.note: A stormy summer, then a fine finish, gave a good, approachable vintage of soft, forward wines. Mature now; drink up.

1999.note: A large crop of generous, soft wines that drank early and charmingly, overshadowed by the millennium hype. Mature now; drink up.

1998.note: A good, consistent vintage, widely declared, with ripe fruit and decent acidity. Mature now and best drunk over the next few years.

1997.note: A good vintage of moderate depth from a warm summer, declared by some houses. Past its best for most bottles; prestige cuvées excepted.

1996.note: Very high acidity and high ripeness together made a legendary but polarising vintage; some bottles have aged fast while others are thrilling. Mature now.

1995.note: A very good, balanced vintage overshadowed by 1996, and often more reliable today because its acidity and fruit are in step. Mature now; drink up.

1994.note: A rainy harvest gave dilute, rot-affected grapes and only a handful of houses released a vintage. Past their best now.

1993.note: Rain at harvest made an uneven vintage, with some decent wines from the best houses and Chardonnay villages. Past its best now.

1992.note: A large, light crop from a wet season, with few vintage declarations and little ageing potential. Past its best now.

1991.note: Spring frost and a small crop of lean grapes; few houses declared a vintage. Past its best now for all but a handful of bottles.

1990.note: A warm, sunny year of rich, ripe, great wines, widely declared and long admired. Mature now; well-stored bottles are lovely but should be drunk.

1988.note: A classic, high-acid, long-lived vintage, slower to develop than 1989 or 1990 and often finer. Mature and splendid now, especially from magnum.

1985.note: A great vintage after a harsh winter killed many vines and cut the crop. Mature now; drink up from good provenance.

1982.note: A large, ripe, generous vintage that was delicious young and has aged well. Mature now; drink up from good provenance.

1979.note: An elegant, fine vintage from a late, cool season. Past its best for most bottles, though prestige cuvées can still be lovely.

1976.note: A hot, drought year of rich, ripe, low-acid wines. Past its best for most bottles; magnums of prestige cuvées survive.

1971.note: A small crop of fine, elegant, well-balanced wines. Past its best for most bottles; perfectly stored ones can be ethereal.

1964.note: A great, rich vintage from a warm, sunny year, widely declared by the grandes marques. Past its best for most bottles; perfectly stored magnums survive.

1928.note: A legendary year for Champagne, among the greatest of the century. Past its best for nearly all bottles; a museum piece now.

2024.note: A wet, mildew-ridden season tested growers at the northern end, where Côte-Rôtie and Condrieu were described as early-drinking. Cornas and Saint-Péray turned out charming and elegant. Lighter Syrah with bright acidity overall.

2023.note: A troublesome climate of spring rain then summer heat gave varied results. The best Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie are ripe and generous, others are heavy or dilute. Choose growers carefully.

2022.note: A hot, dry year that was much better than 2021. Hermitage is more majestic than elegant, Côte-Rôtie needs years to come round, and Saint-Joseph excelled in both colours.

2021.note: April frost and a cool, damp summer gave lighter, peppery, fresh Syrah with modest alcohol, a throwback to older vintages. Crozes and Saint-Joseph are drinking now.

2020.note: A hot, dry summer yet fresh, well-balanced reds with ripe tannins and good acidity. Very good across the appellations; leading wines are still young.

2019.note: Hot and dry, producing powerful, statuesque Hermitage and dense Côte-Rôtie. The best will last for decades; Condrieu was less successful.

2018.note: A hot, generous year with healthy grapes. Ripe, rich, deeply fruited Syrah with plush tannins and enough freshness. Excellent from top to bottom; leading wines are just opening.

2017.note: Drought and heat gave a small crop of concentrated, tannic, powerful reds. Very good; the best need more time to soften.

2016.note: A cooler, balanced year of classic, perfumed, elegant Syrah with fine tannins; Côte-Rôtie was especially fine. Opening now, with the top Hermitage needing a few more years.

2015.note: A hot, dry year that produced great, powerful, concentrated Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie with ripe tannins and good acidity. Leading wines are only now becoming approachable.

2014.note: A wet summer and harvest rain gave lighter, fresher, peppery reds for medium-term drinking. Crozes and Saint-Joseph are ready; Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie are drinking well now.

2013.note: A cold spring and late harvest gave a small crop of fresh, structured, classic Syrah with vivid acidity. Very good and at its peak.

2012.note: A balanced season gave fresh, supple, very good reds with bright black fruit and moderate tannins. At their peak now, with the best Hermitage holding for another decade.

2011.note: A warm spring and a cool summer gave soft, forward, attractive reds for early drinking, with less depth than 2010. Mature now; enjoy them rather than wait.

2010.note: A cool, dry year that gave great, structured, fresh Syrah of real depth and purity. Leading wines are at an early peak and will last decades.

2009.note: A hot, sunny year of ripe, rich, great reds with sweet fruit and firm tannins. At its peak and holding.

2008.note: A wet summer and rot made a light, difficult vintage. Most wines should have been drunk; a few Hermitages survive.

2007.note: A cool summer and a fine September gave fresh, good, elegant reds; Côte-Rôtie was especially pleasing. Mature now and drinking well, with no further gains to come.

2006.note: A warm year of ripe, attractive, well-balanced reds with sweet fruit and supple tannins. Mature and drinking well now; Hermitage from top growers will hold for years.

2005.note: A dry year of great, deeply structured, tannic reds that took years to open. At their peak now, and Hermitage from leading growers has decades left.

2004.note: A balanced, medium-bodied vintage of fresh, peppery Syrah with moderate tannins. Mature now; drink over the next few years while the fruit remains.

2003.note: The heatwave produced powerful, ripe, tannic Syrah; some Hermitage is legendary, other wines feel cooked. Mature; drink most, keep the best.

2002.note: Torrential rain and floods in September ruined much of the crop and growers struggled with rot. Light, weak reds, now past their best almost everywhere.

2001.note: A classic, structured, fresh vintage with fine tannins and bright acidity, long underrated next to 1999. Mature and holding well at the top.

2000.note: A warm, generous year of soft, good reds that drank early and lacked the grip of 1999. Mature now; drink up the remaining bottles.

1999.note: A great, ripe, balanced vintage; Côte-Rôtie was exceptional and Hermitage deep and sweet-fruited. Mature and splendid now, with the best holding for years.

1998.note: Firm, tannic, powerful reds from a hot summer; Hermitage was especially strong. Mature now, the tannins finally resolved, and drinking well.

1997.note: A warm year of ripe, soft, low-acid reds that charmed early but lacked structure. Drink up now; few will improve.

1996.note: A cool year with high acidity gave lean, sometimes green Syrah that never fully filled out. Mature now; drink up the survivors.

1995.note: A firm, structured vintage with good acidity and depth, slow to open. Mature and holding at the top; lesser wines should be drunk.

1994.note: A hot summer spoiled by September rain gave uneven reds with some good Hermitage. Past their best now for most wines.

1993.note: A very wet harvest and widespread rot made a poor vintage across the north. Long past its best. Its drinking window closed around 2010; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1992.note: A wet year of light, dilute reds with little ageing potential. Long past its best. Its drinking window closed around 2010; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1991.note: A good year in which Côte-Rôtie was arguably finer than in 1990, with perfumed, balanced Syrah. Drink up now; well-kept bottles are lovely.

1990.note: A hot year of great, powerful Hermitage; the La Chapelle and Chave wines are legends. Mature now and still vigorous.

1989.note: A hot year of great, rich Hermitage and Cornas with deep fruit and firm tannins. Mature now and holding from good cellars.

1988.note: A classic, structured vintage, especially fine in Côte-Rôtie, where Guigal's single vineyards excelled. Mature now; drink up. The window closes around 2030, so open remaining bottles soon.

1985.note: Ripe, charming reds that drank well early and aged gracefully, especially in Côte-Rôtie. Past their best for most; drink any remaining bottles.

1983.note: Hard, tannic Hermitage that needed decades to soften and divided opinion. Past for most wines; great bottles are austere but alive.

1978.note: A legendary Northern Rhône year of power, balance and longevity, from Hermitage to Côte-Rôtie. Drink perfectly stored bottles now. The window closes around 2030, so open remaining bottles soon.

1961.note: The year of the mythical Hermitage La Chapelle 1961, one of the great wines of the century. Treat surviving bottles as historic artefacts; condition is everything.

2024.note: An outlier year for the south, cooler and wetter than recent vintages, with uneven results. Lighter, fresher reds with moderate alcohol; some charming, some dilute. Expect early drinking.

2023.note: Drought and heat gave ripe, soft reds made for immediate pleasure; Gigondas and Vacqueyras show softer tannins, and Châteauneuf whites are the ones to watch.

2022.note: A drought year that surprised: Châteauneuf-du-Pape was the best-performing appellation in the Rhône, with ripe, balanced, fresh reds. A vintage for reds.

2021.note: April frost and a cool year gave lighter, fresher, lower-alcohol reds with bright fruit. Attractive now and over the next decade.

2020.note: A warm, dry year that kept freshness. Ripe, juicy, well-balanced reds with supple tannins, very good across the south and drinking from early on.

2019.note: Châteauneuf-du-Pape combined elegance with power and outperformed its neighbours. Rich, ripe, balanced reds with fine tannins and long lives ahead.

2018.note: Severe mildew cut Grenache yields, then a hot summer ripened the rest. Rich, ripe, sometimes very alcoholic wines; uneven but often very good.

2017.note: Coulure on Grenache and drought gave a small crop of concentrated, tannic, dark reds. Very good; the best Châteauneufs still need a few years.

2016.note: A great, balanced, ripe and fresh vintage, among the finest ever for Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Gigondas. Opening now with decades ahead.

2015.note: A hot, dry year of ripe, structured, generous reds with firm tannins. Drinking well now and holding for another decade at the top.

2014.note: A wet summer and harvest rain gave lighter, fresher reds with soft tannins. Mature now; drink over the next few years.

2013.note: Grenache coulure and a late harvest made a small crop of fresh, Syrah-marked reds with good acidity. Mature now and drinking well.

2012.note: A balanced season gave very good, supple, fresh reds with bright fruit and moderate alcohol. At their peak now. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2017 to 2035.

2011.note: A warm year of soft, forward, attractive reds without great depth. Mature now; drink up. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2015 to 2030.

2010.note: A cool, dry, small vintage of great, structured, fresh reds of real depth and purity. At its peak and holding for many years.

2009.note: A hot, dry year of ripe, rich reds with soft tannins and generous alcohol. Mature and drinking well now. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2014 to 2035.

2008.note: A wet year of light, early-drinking reds with modest concentration. Past their best now; finish any remaining bottles. Its drinking window closed around 2022; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2007.note: A sunny, Mistral-dried year of lush, ripe, great Grenache with sweet fruit and velvety tannins. At its peak now and holding.

2006.note: A ripe, balanced, very good vintage with fresher acidity than 2007. Mature now and drinking well. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2012 to 2032.

2005.note: A dry year of great, tannic, structured reds that needed patience. At their peak now, with top Châteauneuf holding for years.

2004.note: A cooler year of elegant, fresh, medium-bodied reds. Mature now; drink up over the next couple of years. The window closes around 2028, so open remaining bottles soon.

2003.note: The heatwave gave rich, high-alcohol reds, some baked, some excellent. Mature now; drink up rather than wait. The window closes around 2028, so open remaining bottles soon.

2002.note: Torrential rain and floods on 8 and 9 September devastated Châteauneuf-du-Pape and much of the south. Few wines of note; past their best.

2001.note: A classic, structured vintage with fine tannins and freshness, often preferred to 2000 by purists. Mature and holding well. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2008 to 2032.

2000.note: A ripe, generous vintage of sweet-fruited, soft reds. Mature now; drink up the remaining bottles. The window closes around 2028, so open remaining bottles soon.

1999.note: A balanced, good vintage of medium weight and fresh fruit. Past its best for most wines now; top Châteauneuf can still please.

1998.note: A great Grenache year of ripe, rich, opulent reds, the best southern vintage of the decade. Mature now; drink up.

1997.note: A light, early-drinking vintage with soft fruit and little structure. Long past its best. Its drinking window closed around 2012; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1996.note: A cool, wet year of lean, high-acid reds with little charm. Long past its best. Its drinking window closed around 2012; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1995.note: A firm, very good vintage with good structure and acidity. Past its best for most wines; great estates survive. Its drinking window closed around 2025; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1994.note: A hot summer and rain at harvest made uneven reds. Past their best now. Its drinking window closed around 2018; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1993.note: Harvest rain gave dilute, light wines with little ageing potential. Long past their best. Its drinking window closed around 2010; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1992.note: Floods in September and a wet harvest gave weak, dilute wines. Long past their best. Its drinking window closed around 2010; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1991.note: A light vintage, overshadowed by the north, with soft, short-lived reds. Long past its best. Its drinking window closed around 2008; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1990.note: A hot year of great, rich Châteauneuf, with Rayas and Beaucastel legendary. Drink up now from good cellars. The window closes around 2030, so open remaining bottles soon.

1989.note: A great, structured vintage, Beaucastel especially famed for its depth and longevity. Drink up now from good cellars. The window closes around 2030, so open remaining bottles soon.

1978.note: A legendary southern vintage of power and longevity. Past its best for most wines; great bottles of Châteauneuf survive. Its drinking window closed around 2025; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2024.note: Spring frost, a wet summer and mildew cut Chenin yields sharply in Touraine and Anjou. Mostly dry and sparkling wines with high acidity; little or no moelleux. Choose top growers.

2023.note: A large crop ripened in a hot September. Ripe, open, generous dry and off-dry Chenin; some moelleux in Vouvray and the Layon. Good, early-maturing year.

2022.note: A hot, dry year of ripe, concentrated Chenin with better acidity than feared. Good demi-sec and some moelleux; Savennières is rich and firm.

2021.note: Devastating April frost and a cool, wet summer made a tiny crop of tense, high-acid Chenin, largely sec and sparkling. Lean but pure.

2020.note: A hot, early year with ripe, rich Chenin and some botrytis; demi-sec and moelleux were made. Very good; dry wines are opening.

2019.note: Frost and heatwaves reduced yields and concentrated the wines. Energetic, concentrated dry Chenin with fine acidity and some sweet wines; drinking well and will keep.

2018.note: A hot, healthy, generous year that allowed demi-sec and moelleux across Vouvray, Montlouis and the Layon. Rich, ripe and long-lived.

2017.note: Frost cut the crop; the dry wines are good, balanced and fresh with lively acidity. Little sweet wine was made; mature now.

2016.note: The April frost and mildew destroyed much of the crop. Small volumes of lean, dry Chenin. Drink up the lighter cuvées.

2015.note: A warm, dry summer and a fine autumn produced the full range from sec to moelleux, rich and balanced. A superb vintage.

2014.note: A cool summer and a glorious autumn gave classic, mineral, dry and off-dry Chenin with great tension. Very good and at its peak now.

2013.note: Hail struck Vouvray in June, and rot spread in a late, wet harvest. A poor year; drink any remaining bottles.

2012.note: Frost, mildew and a cool summer gave small volumes of lean Chenin. Past its best for most wines, though top Savennières is holding.

2011.note: An early, uneven year with some botrytis in Anjou and the Layon. Good rather than great; mature now and best drunk.

2010.note: A cool, classic year of high-acid, mineral dry Chenin and some fine sweet wines. Mature and holding, the dry wines honeyed and firm.

2009.note: A warm year of ripe, generous Chenin with good demi-sec and moelleux. Mature and drinking well, with the sweet wines holding longest.

2008.note: A cool year of high-acid dry Chenin that needed time to open. Mature now, the acidity still bright, and best drunk soon.

2007.note: A wet summer brought rot, but Layon botrytis was good in places. Mature now; dry wines should be drunk. The window closes around 2028, so open remaining bottles soon.

2006.note: A hot July and a wet August gave uneven wines with some good botrytis in the sweet appellations. Drink up now.

2005.note: A great vintage across the board, from powerful dry Savennières to rich, balanced moelleux. At its peak and holding for decades.

2004.note: A cool, large crop of fresh, dry Chenin with little sweet wine. Mature now; drink up. Its drinking window closed around 2025; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2003.note: The heatwave gave rich, ripe Chenin and fine moelleux, sometimes low in acidity. Mature now; the sweet wines will keep longer.

2002.note: A cool, sunny autumn gave classic, fine Chenin with high acidity and some sweet wine. Mature and holding well. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2007 to 2035.

2001.note: A mixed year with good dry and some sweet wines in Anjou. Mature now; drink the dry wines. The window closes around 2028, so open remaining bottles soon.

2000.note: A wet harvest gave weak, dilute wines with little sweet Chenin. Past their best now. Its drinking window closed around 2020; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1999.note: Harvest rain and rot spoiled much of the crop. Past their best now except a few moelleux. Its drinking window closed around 2018; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1998.note: A wet autumn and modest, lean wines. Past their best now. Its drinking window closed around 2018; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1997.note: A great year for moelleux, rich and balanced, and fine dry Chenin from a warm, dry autumn. Mature and splendid.

1996.note: High sugar and high acidity together gave great, long-lived Chenin in all styles. Mature and splendid, the sweet wines still youthful.

1995.note: A very good year for moelleux, overshadowed by 1996 and 1997 but long-lived. Mature and holding. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2001 to 2040.

1994.note: A wet harvest gave lean, dilute wines with little sweet Chenin. Past its best now. Its drinking window closed around 2015; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1993.note: A wet harvest gave light wines and few moelleux of note. Past its best now. Its drinking window closed around 2012; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1992.note: A large, light crop with little concentration. Past its best now. Its drinking window closed around 2010; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1991.note: Frost destroyed much of the crop in April. What remains is long past its best. Its drinking window closed around 2008; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1990.note: A hot year of great moelleux and rich dry Chenin, the middle of a great trio. Mature and splendid, with decades left for the sweet wines.

1989.note: A hot year of great, rich, botrytised moelleux in Vouvray and the Layon. Mature and splendid, with decades left. Its drinking window runs roughly from 1995 to 2050.

1976.note: A hot drought year of rich, ripe sweet Chenin. Mature now; the best moelleux are still vigorous. Its drinking window runs roughly from 1985 to 2040.

1959.note: A legendary year for sweet Vouvray, still found in the cellars of old houses such as Huet. Mature and remarkable.

1947.note: One of the greatest years for sweet Loire Chenin, rich and incredibly long-lived. Mature and remarkable from good cellars. Its drinking window runs roughly from 1960 to 2050.

1921.note: A legendary hot year for sweet Loire Chenin, among the oldest wines still occasionally released from producer cellars. Mature; provenance decides.

2024.note: Frost, a cool, rainy summer and heavy mildew pressure cut yields across Touraine and Saumur. Light, crunchy, low-alcohol Cabernet Franc for early drinking; top cuvées are leaner than usual.

2023.note: A large crop finished in a hot September. Ripe, juicy, supple Cabernet Franc with soft tannins, attractive young; the best cuvées have more depth and will keep a decade.

2022.note: A hot, dry year that fully ripened Cabernet Franc on gravel and limestone alike. Deep, ripe, velvety reds without greenness; top Chinon and Bourgueil will age well.

2021.note: April frost and a cool, damp summer gave a small crop of lean, fresh, sometimes leafy reds with high acidity. Drink the lighter cuvées now.

2020.note: A hot, early year of ripe, concentrated Cabernet Franc with good freshness. Very good; top cuvées are opening now and will hold.

2019.note: Frost and heatwaves cut yields, giving dense, ripe, concentrated reds with fine tannins. Very good and drinking well from the better cuvées.

2018.note: A hot, healthy, generous year of fully ripe, plush, deeply coloured Cabernet Franc. A great Loire red vintage, at its peak and holding.

2017.note: The April frost cut volumes; what remained made fresh, balanced, medium-weight reds with crunchy fruit. Good and mature now. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2020 to 2032.

2016.note: Frost and mildew devastated parts of Touraine, but a fine summer ripened the survivors into good, balanced reds. Mature now.

2015.note: A warm, dry year of great, ripe, concentrated Cabernet Franc with fine tannins. At its peak, with the best Chinon holding for years.

2014.note: A cool summer and a fine autumn gave classic, fresh, well-structured reds with ripe tannins. Very good and at its peak now.

2013.note: A cold, wet year left Cabernet Franc underripe and green. Light, leafy reds; past their best now. Its drinking window closed around 2024; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2012.note: Frost, mildew and a cool summer gave small volumes of lean, light reds. Past their best now. Its drinking window closed around 2025; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2011.note: An early, uneven year of supple, attractive reds for medium-term drinking. Mature now; drink up. The window closes around 2026, so open remaining bottles soon.

2010.note: A cool, dry year of fresh, structured, classic Cabernet Franc with good depth. Mature and drinking well. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2014 to 2032.

2009.note: A warm year of ripe, generous, rounded reds with soft tannins. Mature and drinking well now. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2013 to 2032.

2008.note: A cool year of firm, high-acid reds that softened slowly. Mature now; drink up. The window closes around 2028, so open remaining bottles soon.

2007.note: A wet summer gave light, leafy, short-lived reds. Past their best now. Its drinking window closed around 2020; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2006.note: A hot July, a wet August and some rot made uneven reds. Past their best for most cuvées. Its drinking window closed around 2024; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2005.note: A dry, sunny year of great, ripe, deeply structured Cabernet Franc. Mature and still vigorous at the top estates. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2010 to 2035.

2004.note: A large, cool crop of fresh, lighter reds. Past their best for most cuvées now. Its drinking window closed around 2022; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2003.note: The heatwave ripened Cabernet Franc fully, giving rich, warm reds, some low in acidity. Mature now; drink up. The window closes around 2028, so open remaining bottles soon.

2002.note: A cool summer and a sunny autumn gave classic, fresh, structured reds. Mature now; drink up. The window closes around 2026, so open remaining bottles soon.

2001.note: A mixed year of fresh, medium-weight reds. Past their best now for nearly all cuvées. Its drinking window closed around 2020; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

2000.note: A good year of supple, forward reds that drank well young. Past their best now. Its drinking window closed around 2018; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1999.note: Rain at harvest diluted the reds and left them lean. Long past their best. Its drinking window closed around 2014; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1998.note: A wet September gave light, early-drinking reds. Long past their best. Its drinking window closed around 2014; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1997.note: A warm year of ripe, soft, generous reds. Past their best for most cuvées; old-vine Chinon may survive. Its drinking window closed around 2025; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1996.note: A cool, sunny, windy year gave great, firm, high-acid reds that aged superbly. Drink up now from good cellars. The window closes around 2030, so open remaining bottles soon.

1995.note: A ripe, very good year for reds with firm structure. Past its best for most cuvées now. Its drinking window closed around 2022; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1994.note: A wet harvest gave weak, dilute reds. Long past their best. Its drinking window closed around 2010; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1993.note: A wet harvest gave weak, light reds. Long past their best. Its drinking window closed around 2010; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1992.note: A light, large crop with little depth. Long past its best. Its drinking window closed around 2008; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1991.note: Spring frost cut the crop and the survivors were lean. Long past their best. Its drinking window closed around 2008; treat any survivor as a curiosity.

1990.note: A hot year of great, ripe, concentrated reds, the finest of the era for Chinon and Bourgueil. Drink up now from good cellars.

1989.note: A hot year of great, ripe reds with sweet fruit and firm tannins. Drink up now from good cellars. The window closes around 2030, so open remaining bottles soon.

2024.note: A cool, rainy year with mildew and a smaller crop. Fresh, lighter, high-acid wines; Riesling is crisp and saline, aromatic varieties lighter than usual. Few late-harvest wines.

2023.note: A warm summer and a sunny September gave ripe, balanced, aromatic wines with good acidity. Very good across the varieties; some VT.

2022.note: A hot, dry year that kept freshness thanks to cool nights and old vines. Ripe, generous wines; Riesling grand crus are deep and balanced.

2021.note: Frost, a wet summer and mildew cut yields. Tense, high-acid, classic Riesling, lean but pure, with fewer sweet wines than usual. Grand crus are just opening.

2020.note: A hot, early year of ripe, aromatic wines with surprising freshness from cool nights. Very good across the varieties; grand crus are opening now.

2019.note: A hot summer and a small crop gave concentrated, vibrant, balanced wines with fine acidity. An excellent vintage for Riesling grand crus.

2018.note: A hot, generous year of ripe, rich wines with soft acidity; the best grand crus kept balance. Drinking well now; drink the aromatic varieties first.

2017.note: Spring frost reduced the crop, but the remaining grapes made excellent, pure, concentrated wines with fine acidity. A top vintage for Riesling, now opening.

2016.note: A wet spring and a fine late summer gave classic, fresh, balanced wines of medium weight. Very good and drinking well now.

2015.note: A hot, dry year of rich, concentrated wines with good acidity on limestone and granite. Great for grand crus and VT.

2014.note: Fruit flies and rot troubled the harvest, but Riesling held up with fresh, linear, saline wines. Good, and mature now.

2013.note: A cold spring and a late harvest gave high-acid, lean but classic Riesling that has softened with age. Good; mature now.

2012.note: A small crop of balanced, concentrated wines with ripe fruit and fresh acidity. Very good and mature now. Its drinking window runs roughly from 2016 to 2032.

2011.note: An early, warm year of soft, forward, aromatic wines. Mature now; drink up, especially Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris. The window closes around 2026, so open remaining bottles soon.

2010.note: A tiny crop with very high acidity gave great, long-lived, piercing Riesling. Mature and splendid now, with years left for grand crus.
